title: Neurons and Signals
hook: Your every thought, twitch, and feeling rides on tiny electrical pulses fired by neurons — and leaps the gaps between them as bursts of chemicals.
key_points: Neurons are specialized cells that carry information as fast electrical signals.
A signal travels down a neuron as a wave of electrical change called an action potential.
Where two neurons meet — a synapse — the signal usually crosses as chemical messengers called neurotransmitters.
Billions of neurons wired together form the networks behind sensing, moving, and thinking.
content_html: A neuron is a cell built for communication. Instead of just sitting in a tissue doing chemistry, it carries information as quick electrical pulses, then hands that information off to the next cell. String billions of these together and you get a nervous system — the network behind everything you sense, feel, and do.
extra_html: A typical neuron has branchy arms (dendrites) that collect incoming signals, a cell body, and a long fiber (the axon) that carries the outgoing signal. When a neuron fires, a wave of electrical change called an action potential sweeps down the axon. But neurons don't quite touch — there's a microscopic gap called a synapse. To cross it, the signal becomes chemical: the axon tip releases neurotransmitters that float across and trigger the next neuron. This electrical-then-chemical relay, repeated across trillions of connections, is how the NIH's NINDS describes the basic working of the brain and nerves.

related.title: The Brain
related.hook: Three pounds of folded tissue runs the whole show — thinking, balance, breathing, memory — divided into regions that each handle a different part of the job.

related.title: The Senses
related.hook: Light, sound, chemicals, and pressure can't enter your brain directly — your senses translate all of them into the one language your neurons understand: electrical signals.

flashcards.prompt: What kind of signal travels down the length of a neuron?
flashcards.back_html: An electrical signal called an action potential — a brief wave of voltage change that races along the neuron from one end to the other.

flashcards.prompt: How does a signal usually cross the gap between two neurons?

choices.text: Chemical messengers (neurotransmitters) released into the synapse
A metal wire connecting the two cells
The neurons physically merge into one cell

flashcards.explanation_html: At a synapse, the arriving signal triggers the release of neurotransmitters, which drift across the tiny gap and pass the message to the next neuron.

choices.text: A specialized cell that carries information as electrical signals
A type of blood cell that fights infection
A molecule that stores genetic instructions

flashcards.explanation_html: Neurons are the working cells of the nervous system, built to receive, conduct, and pass on signals at high speed.
